title: Smart pointers
summary: unique_ptr, shared_ptr and weak_ptr: ownership the compiler enforces.

cards.title: Owners clean up
cards.body: A **smart pointer** is an object that owns heap memory and deletes it automatically in its destructor. This trick (tie a resource to an object's lifetime) is called **RAII**, and it's the heart of modern C++.

cards.title: The code
cards.body: `std::move` doesn't move anything by itself. It says "you may steal from this". The unique_ptr move constructor then takes the address and leaves gold empty. A unique_ptr is usually the same size as a raw pointer: safety for free.

cards.title: shared_ptr: counted owners
cards.body: Every copy adds an owner, every destroyed copy removes one. At zero, the object is deleted.

cards.title: weak_ptr: look, don't own
cards.body: Two objects that own each other with shared_ptr would never reach a count of 0. A weak_ptr link breaks the cycle.

cards.title: Which one?
cards.body:
- Default to **unique_ptr**. Most things have one clear owner (a level owns its entities).
- **shared_ptr** only when ownership is truly shared. It costs a control block and atomic counting on every copy.
- **weak_ptr** for back-links and observers: "I want to reach it if it still exists."
- Raw pointers and references are still fine for **non-owning** access.

cards.question: Does this compile?
cards.code:
auto a = std::make_unique<int>(1);
auto b = a;
choices: No: a unique_ptr can't be copied
cards.explain: Copying would create two owners. You must write `auto b = std::move(a);`, after which a is empty.

cards.question: What does this print?
cards.explain: a and b are owners. c was a third owner but died at the end of its block, leaving 2.

cards.title: Build it: an inventory that owns its items
cards.body: Create items with `make_unique`, move them into a bag, and add up their power. No `new`, no `delete`.
